title: Between-User Collapse Under Popularity-Biased Feedback:A Centered-Covariance Theorem and Computable Phase Boundary

paper.title: Between-User Collapse Under Popularity-Biased Feedback: A Centered-Covariance Theorem and Computable Phase Boundary
paper.abstract: Abstract. We study how popularity-biased BPR training reshapes the between-user geometry of collaborative-filtering embeddings. We work with the mean-centered user covariance C = 1 n ​ U ⊤ ​ H ​ U C=\tfrac{1}{n}U^{\top}HU , the object that measures how distinguishable users are from one another, as opposed to the uncentered second moment used in prior work. We prove that under popularity-biased feedback with stationary items, C C converges to a steady state proportional to the item-noise covariance Q Q . Thus between-user spread collapses toward a noise floor. We derive a closed-form, computable phase boundary in the training hyperparameters ( α , λ neg , γ , d ) (\alpha,\lambda_{\mathrm{neg}},\gamma,d) separating contraction from expansion, and validate both directional predictions on MovieLens-25M. We then examine the limits of the effect. At deployment-scale regularization the predicted contraction is real and policy-driven but small, and it is not reflected in any recommendation-level metric we measured. The α \alpha -driven anisotropic-collapse mechanism operates only at regularization strengths that degrade the recommender. A deployment-time restoration intervention derived from the theory does not improve recommendation quality. The boundary is computable from a trained model’s embeddings, item interaction counts, and training hyperparameters, so a practitioner can check whether a deployed system sits in the strong-collapse regime without simulating the feedback loop. In our experiments the boundary places deployable settings far from that regime.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Recommendation feedback loops homogenize users. Training on algorithmically confounded data homogenizes behavior without increasing utility ( Chaney et al., 2018 ) , and iterated retraining makes popularity bias stronger ( Mansoury et al., 2020 ) . These are behavioral accounts of a long-term consequence. What is less understood is how popularity-biased training reshapes the geometry of the user embedding space over time, and we lack a good test of whether that geometric effect has measurable recommendation-level consequences. There is a growing line of work that studies embedding collapse in collaborative filtering ( Peng et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Loveland et al., 2025b ) , echoing dimensional collapse in contrastive self-supervised learning ( Jing et al., 2022 ) . All of it operates on the uncentered embedding matrix or its second moment Σ = 1 n ​ U ⊤ ​ U \Sigma=\tfrac{1}{n}U^{\top}U , which conflates two distinct phenomena. Under popularity bias, user embeddings drift together toward a shared “popularity direction”, which is a mean-drift effect recently characterized analytically ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . A decline in the stable rank of the uncentered matrix ( Loveland et al., 2025b ) is consistent with mean drift alone, meaning users can move together without becoming more similar to one another . User homogenization means recommendations becoming identical across users , not just worse on average, and is a property of the centered covariance C = Σ − 𝐮 ¯ ​ 𝐮 ¯ ⊤ C=\Sigma-\bar{\mathbf{u}}\bar{\mathbf{u}}^{\top} , which no prior work analyzes under feedback. The phase boundary we derive only needs a trained model’s embeddings, item interaction counts, and training hyperparameters, so a practitioner can determine whether a system sits in the strong-collapse regime before worrying about geometric homogenization. Contributions. (1) A theorem on the centered (between-user) covariance: under popularity-biased BPR feedback with stationary items, C C converges to a steady state exactly proportional to the item-noise covariance Q Q . Centering removes the popularity-drift component, and between-user spread collapses toward a noise floor whose anisotropy is that of Q Q . (2) A closed-form phase boundary in ( α , λ neg , γ , d ) (\alpha,\lambda_{\mathrm{neg}},\gamma,d) , computable from a trained embedding matrix, item counts, and hyperparameters, separating contraction from expansion regimes. We validate both directions on MovieLens-25M. (3) An empirical scoping showing that at deployable regularization the contraction is real and policy-driven but not reflected in recommendation metrics in our setup, that the α \alpha -driven anisotropy mechanism is inert at deployable settings, and a theory-derived restoration intervention that slightly hurts accuracy.

sections.heading: 2. Related Work
sections.text: Embedding collapse in CF (uncentered, training-time). DirectSpec ( Peng et al., 2025 ) balances the embedding spectrum during training (alignment as low-pass, negative sampling as high-pass filter). nCL ( Chen et al., 2024 ) prevents dimensional collapse via an alignment-plus-compactness (coding-rate) objective. Zhang et al. ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) show graph convolution shrinks the singular space and counteract it with a LogDet regularizer. Loveland et al. ( Loveland et al., 2025b ) show alignment lowers the stable rank of the raw user/item matrices. That is an uncentered object whose decline is consistent with pure mean drift. Their companion result shows weight decay encodes popularity into embedding magnitudes ( Loveland et al., 2025a ) , which is a norm-level effect. None of these analyze the mean-centered between-user covariance, and none derive a contraction/expansion phase boundary in the training hyperparameters. Liu et al. ( Liu et al., 2026 ) prove BPR organizes item embeddings along a dominant popularity direction and propose a directional correction (DDC). Their analysis focuses on the mean-drift component, while our result characterizes what happens to between-user spread after the mean drifts. The drift term is eliminated exactly in our analysis. Simulation studies ( Chaney et al., 2018 ; Mansoury et al., 2020 ) establish the behavioral consequence. We provide the representational mechanism and test whether the geometric effect has behavioral consequences at deployable settings. The distinction that does the work is centering. Every prior analysis of collapse in collaborative filtering studies an uncentered object, and an uncentered spectrum falls when users translate together just as it falls when they converge on each other. The two are different claims about a recommender, and only the second is homogenization.

sections.text: Corollary 4.2 is meant to be run, so we state the procedure. (2) Form C 0 = 1 | ℳ κ | ​ U ℳ κ ⊤ ​ H ​ U ℳ κ C^{0}=\tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{M}_{\kappa}|}U_{\mathcal{M}_{\kappa}}^{\top}HU_{\mathcal{M}_{\kappa}} on the retained rows and take log det ( C 0 + ε I ) \log\det(C^{0}+\varepsilon I) . sections.heading: 5. Empirical Findings
sections.text: Setup. All experiments use MovieLens-25M with d = 64 d=64 , n = 162,541 n=162{,}541 users, and m = 59,047 m=59{,}047 items. The mainstream set ℳ κ \mathcal{M}_{\kappa} with κ = 3.0 \kappa=3.0 gives 63,854 63{,}854 users, and the fitted popularity exponent is α ^ = 1.11 \hat{\alpha}=1.11 ( R 2 = 0.953 R^{2}=0.953 ). We use λ neg = 1 \lambda_{\mathrm{neg}}=1 , η = 0.001 \eta=0.001 , the Adam optimizer, and an ε = 10 − 6 \varepsilon=10^{-6} ridge throughout.

sections.heading: 5.1. Phase boundary validation
sections.text: With items frozen, Assumption 4 is satisfied by construction. We measure log det Q = − 405.77 \log\det Q=-405.77 , and the corollary’s right-hand side evaluates to − 30.91 -30.91 at γ = 0.1 \gamma=0.1 and − 472.89 -472.89 at γ = 10 − 4 \gamma=10^{-4} , predicting contraction at γ = 0.1 \gamma=0.1 (margin + 374.87 +374.87 ) and expansion at γ = 10 − 4 \gamma=10^{-4} (margin − 67.12 -67.12 ). Frozen-item training shows that V C V_{C} contracts at γ = 0.1 \gamma=0.1 ( − 496.82 → − 592.44 -496.82\to-592.44 , − 19.25 % -19.25\% ) and expands at γ = 10 − 4 \gamma=10^{-4} ( + 28.55 % +28.55\% , Figure 1 ). sections.text: Regressing log ⁡ λ k ​ ( C ∗ ) \log\lambda_{k}(C^{*}) on log ⁡ μ k ​ ( Q ) \log\mu_{k}(Q) at the γ = 0.1 \gamma=0.1 plateau yields slope 0.954 0.954 , R 2 = 0.990 R^{2}=0.990 (Figure 2 ), robust to ε \varepsilon -tail removal ( 0 0 of 64 64 eigenvalues in the ε \varepsilon tail). This indicates the Q 1 Q^{1} law of Theorem 4.1 persists under Adam (rather than a Q 1 / 2 Q^{1/2} law). The deviation is not specific to Adam. In a fully synthetic SGD environment satisfying every assumption, the same regression yields slope 0.926 0.926 with R 2 R^{2} of 0.998 0.998 (Appendix A ), so the compression appears under the theorem’s own optimizer. We attribute it to the state dependence of δ i ​ j \delta_{ij} , which the δ ¯ \bar{\delta} approximation discards. Learning happens the fastest along high-variance item directions, which suppresses noise injection exactly where μ k \mu_{k} is largest. Figure 2. The magnitude, however, is off, and the regression characterizes the offset exactly. sections.heading: 5.3. Behavior at deployable γ \gamma
sections.text: In the full feedback loop at γ = 10 − 4 \gamma=10^{-4} , V C V_{C} declines − 1.75 % -1.75\% over 50 50 rounds with signal-to-noise ≈ 230 \approx 230 across seeds, while a null arm (random recommendations) expands + 4.50 % +4.50\% , matching the corollary’s stationary-item expansion prediction at this γ \gamma and establishing the contraction as policy-driven. However, no recommendation-level metric moves in lockstep with V C V_{C} . Inter-user list similarity falls from ∼ 0.108 {\sim}0.108 to ∼ 0.07 {\sim}0.07 – 0.08 0.08 by rounds 5–10 and flattens (the wrong direction for homogenization), and per-user churn rises to ∼ 0.995 {\sim}0.995 during rounds 0–10 while V C V_{C} is still expanding (drift, not convergence). Additionally, coverage is flat ( 0.0119 → ∼ 0.011 0.0119\to{\sim}0.011 – 0.012 0.012 ) and tail exposure floors at 0.0000 0.0000 by round 3, before the V C V_{C} arc begins, so the setup has limited power to detect tail-side consequences. Although the contraction is detectable, we don’t observe corresponding changes in recommendation metrics.

sections.heading: 5.4. The α \alpha -driven anisotropy mechanism is negligible at deployable γ \gamma
sections.text: Sweeping α ∈ [ 0 , 2 ] \alpha\in[0,2] at γ = 10 − 4 \gamma=10^{-4} , effective rank is flat ( 10.89 10.89 at α = 0 \alpha=0 vs. 10.87 10.87 at α = 2 \alpha=2 ) with healthy accuracy (NDCG@10 ∼ 0.030 {\sim}0.030 ) throughout, and the popularity-alignment share of variance slightly decreases with α \alpha . The α \alpha -driven anisotropic collapse takes place only at model-breaking γ = 0.1 \gamma=0.1 . At deployable γ \gamma the phase boundary is dominated by the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} /prefactor term. (An earlier draft’s mechanism attributing anisotropy to alignment with 𝚽 ⁡ ( α ) \boldsymbol{\Phi}(\alpha) rested on a variance-vs.-squared-mean error that centering removes, and these results are inconsistent with that interpretation.)

sections.heading: 5.5. Evaluation of a theory-derived restoration intervention
sections.text: The theorem suggests a deployment-time restoration of collapsed directions and, at training time, a centered log-det regularizer with gradient 2 n ​ H ​ U ​ ( C + ε ​ I ) − 1 \tfrac{2}{n}HU(C+\varepsilon I)^{-1} that provably raises the steady-state V C V_{C} , but unlike post-hoc stabilization for basis consistency ( Zielnicki and Hsiao, 2025 ) , the goal here is re-inflating collapsed directions. Empirically, the restoration arm yields NDCG@10 = 0.050 =0.050 vs. baseline 0.056 0.056 , so it slightly hurts, with TailNDCG = 0.0000 =0.0000 for both arms (measurement floor, disclosed). This is consistent with Section 5.3 . If between-user contraction has no measurable recommendation-level effects at deployable settings, reversing it shouldn’t improve quality, and empirically it doesn’t.

sections.heading: 5.6. The boundary in a fully synthetic environment
sections.text: We also test the boundary where every assumption holds by construction, with frozen anisotropic items, plain SGD, and all users mainstream (Appendix A ). Above the predicted crossover γ ∗ ≈ 2.3 × 10 − 3 \gamma^{*}\approx 2.3\times 10^{-3} the predicted sign matches at all four grid points, and at γ = 0.1 \gamma=0.1 the predicted plateau is accurate to 1.7 1.7 nats. Below the crossover the theory predicts expansion, but we observe a persistent residual contraction of 8.6 8.6 to 14.6 14.6 percent at one million steps, with δ ¯ \bar{\delta} decaying 20 20 to 23 23 percent against about 3 3 percent above the boundary. The state dependence of δ i ​ j \delta_{ij} therefore adds a contractive force in the fitting regime, so the expansion-side prediction is condition dependent, while the strong-collapse side is reliable in both simulation and on real data.

sections.heading: 6. Limitations
sections.text: Strong contraction manifests only at regularization strengths ( γ = 0.1 \gamma=0.1 ) that degrade the recommender. At deployable γ \gamma it is small and was not reflected in any recommendation-level metric we measured (tail-exposure floor caveat noted). The α \alpha -driven anisotropy mechanism does not operate at deployable γ \gamma . Under Adam the steady-state magnitude deviates by a constant factor, and in simulation the expansion-side prediction fails when the model fits, since the state dependence of δ i ​ j \delta_{ij} adds a contractive force the δ ¯ \bar{\delta} approximation misses (Appendix A ). The theory-motivated intervention did not improve quality. The scope is mainstream users ℳ κ \mathcal{M}_{\kappa} and stationary items, validated by construction rather than in deployment.

sections.heading: 6.1. Single dataset
sections.text: Every number here comes from MovieLens-25M. The dataset has a public-benchmark popularity profile with fitted α ^ = 1.11 \hat{\alpha}=1.11 and R 2 = 0.953 R^{2}=0.953 , which is a reasonable stand-in for a skewed catalog, but representativeness beyond it is an assumption and not a result. Two quantities in the boundary are dataset-dependent in ways we have not measured elsewhere. The first is log det Q \log\det Q , which depends on how the item embedding geometry lines up with the popularity weights, and a catalog with a different tail shape moves it. The second is the coverage of ℳ κ \mathcal{M}_{\kappa} at a given κ \kappa , which was 95.4 % 95.4\% of active users here and would be smaller on a platform with more niche consumption. Neither affects the derivation, and both affect where a given system sits relative to the boundary. Cross-dataset validation on the centered object is future work. We would rather say that plainly than generalize from one dataset.

sections.heading: 7. Conclusion
sections.text: We give a centered-covariance theorem with exact drift cancellation, and steady state C ∗ ∝ Q C^{*}\propto Q , with a phase boundary computable from a trained model’s embeddings, item counts, and hyperparameters. We also see where the mechanism applies and where it doesn’t. The negative results are what make the positive result usable. In our experiments the boundary says deployable settings sit far from the collapse regime, which is worth knowing before spending anything on measuring it.

sections.heading: Below the crossover.
sections.text: The three arms below γ ∗ \gamma^{*} predict expansion but contract persistently, still declining at one million steps, which is two full relaxation times 1 / ( 2 ​ η ​ γ ) 1/(2\eta\gamma) at γ = 10 − 3 \gamma=10^{-3} . The decayed δ ¯ \bar{\delta} cannot account for this. At γ = 10 − 4 \gamma=10^{-4} the fixed point computed with the decayed δ ¯ = 0.383 \bar{\delta}=0.383 sits at − 70.7 -70.7 , far above the observed − 122.0 -122.0 , and the system moves away from it. The cause is the state dependence of δ i ​ j \delta_{ij} itself, which is anticorrelated with 𝐮 \mathbf{u} . Users who already fit an item direction receive smaller updates along it, an extra contractive force the constant- δ ¯ \bar{\delta} approximation leaves out. Consistent with this, δ ¯ \bar{\delta} decays 20 20 to 23 23 percent in the three fitting arms against roughly 3 3 percent at γ = 0.1 \gamma=0.1 , where weight decay keeps scores near zero and the approximation is nearly exact.

sections.heading: What this scopes.
sections.text: The two sides of the boundary are not equally reliable, and the simulation is how we know. Above the crossover the prediction holds in sign at every grid point and in magnitude to 0.11 0.11 nats per dimension, under the theorem’s own optimizer, with every assumption true by construction. Below it the sign prediction fails in a specific and explainable way. Because the failure appears here, in an environment with no confounds, it isn’t an artifact of real data, of Adam, or of the mainstream-user restriction. It is a limitation of the constant- δ ¯ \bar{\delta} approximation in the regime where the model actually fits. A reader deciding whether to trust the boundary on their own system should read it as a reliable detector of the strong-collapse regime and not as a guarantee of expansion below it.

We study how popularity-biased BPR training reshapes the between-user geometry of collaborative-filtering embeddings. We work with the mean-centered user covariance C = 1 n ​ U ⊤ ​ H ​ U C=\tfrac{1}{n}U^{\top}HU , the object that measures how distinguishable users are from one another, as opposed to the uncentered second moment used in prior work. We prove that under popularity-biased feedback with stationary items, C C converges to a steady state proportional to the item-noise covariance Q Q . Thus between-user spread collapses toward a noise floor. We derive a closed-form, computable phase boundary in the training hyperparameters ( α , λ neg , γ , d ) (\alpha,\lambda_{\mathrm{neg}},\gamma,d) separating contraction from expansion, and validate both directional predictions on MovieLens-25M. We then examine the limits of the effect. At deployment-scale regularization the predicted contraction is real and policy-driven but small, and it is not reflected in any recommendation-level metric we measured. The α \alpha -driven anisotropic-collapse mechanism operates only at regularization strengths that degrade the recommender. A deployment-time restoration intervention derived from the theory does not improve recommendation quality. The boundary is computable from a trained model’s embeddings, item interaction counts, and training hyperparameters, so a practitioner can check whether a deployed system sits in the strong-collapse regime without simulating the feedback loop. In our experiments the boundary places deployable settings far from that regime. Keywords: feedback loops, popularity bias, collaborative filtering, embedding collapse, user homogenization, negative results 1. Introduction Recommendation feedback loops homogenize users. Training on algorithmically confounded data homogenizes behavior without increasing utility ( Chaney et al., 2018 ) , and iterated retraining makes popularity bias stronger ( Mansoury et al., 2020 ) . These are behavioral accounts of a long-term consequence. What is less understood is how popularity-biased training reshapes the geometry of the user embedding space over time, and we lack a good test of whether that geometric effect has measurable recommendation-level consequences. There is a growing line of work that studies embedding collapse in collaborative filtering ( Peng et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Loveland et al., 2025b ) , echoing dimensional collapse in contrastive self-supervised learning ( Jing et al., 2022 ) . All of it operates on the uncentered embedding matrix or its second moment Σ = 1 n ​ U ⊤ ​ U \Sigma=\tfrac{1}{n}U^{\top}U , which conflates two distinct phenomena. Under popularity bias, user embeddings drift together toward a shared “popularity direction”, which is a mean-drift effect recently characterized analytically ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . A decline in the stable rank of the uncentered matrix ( Loveland et al., 2025b ) is consistent with mean drift alone, meaning users can move together without becoming more similar to one another . User homogenization means recommendations becoming identical across users , not just worse on average, and is a property of the centered covariance C = Σ − 𝐮 ¯ ​ 𝐮 ¯ ⊤ C=\Sigma-\bar{\mathbf{u}}\bar{\mathbf{u}}^{\top} , which no prior work analyzes under feedback. The phase boundary we derive only needs a trained model’s embeddings, item interaction counts, and training hyperparameters, so a practitioner can determine whether a system sits in the strong-collapse regime before worrying about geometric homogenization. Contributions. (1) A theorem on the centered (between-user) covariance: under popularity-biased BPR feedback with stationary items, C C converges to a steady state exactly proportional to the item-noise covariance Q Q . Centering removes the popularity-drift component, and between-user spread collapses toward a noise floor whose anisotropy is that of Q Q . (2) A closed-form phase boundary in ( α , λ neg , γ , d ) (\alpha,\lambda_{\mathrm{neg}},\gamma,d) , computable from a trained embedding matrix, item counts, and hyperparameters, separating contraction from expansion regimes. We validate both directions on MovieLens-25M. (3) An empirical scoping showing that at deployable regularization the contraction is real and policy-driven but not reflected in recommendation metrics in our setup, that the α \alpha -driven anisotropy mechanism is inert at deployable settings, and a theory-derived restoration intervention that slightly hurts accuracy. 2. Related Work Embedding collapse in CF (uncentered, training-time). DirectSpec ( Peng et al., 2025 ) balances the embedding spectrum during training (alignment as low-pass, negative sampling as high-pass filter). nCL ( Chen et al., 2024 ) prevents dimensional collapse via an alignment-plus-compactness (coding-rate) objective. Zhang et al. ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) show graph convolution shrinks the singular space and counteract it with a LogDet regularizer. Loveland et al. ( Loveland et al., 2025b ) show alignment lowers the stable rank of the raw user/item matrices. That is an uncentered object whose decline is consistent with pure mean drift. Their companion result shows weight decay encodes popularity into embedding magnitudes ( Loveland et al., 2025a ) , which is a norm-level effect. None of these analyze the mean-centered between-user covariance, and none derive a contraction/expansion phase boundary in the training hyperparameters. Liu et al. ( Liu et al., 2026 ) prove BPR organizes item embeddings along a dominant popularity direction and propose a directional correction (DDC). Their analysis focuses on the mean-drift component, while our result characterizes what happens to between-user spread after the mean drifts. The drift term is eliminated exactly in our analysis. Simulation studies ( Chaney et al., 2018 ; Mansoury et al., 2020 ) establish the behavioral consequence. We provide the representational mechanism and test whether the geometric effect has behavioral consequences at deployable settings. The distinction that does the work is centering. Every prior analysis of collapse in collaborative filtering studies an uncentered object, and an uncentered spectrum falls when users translate together just as it falls when they converge on each other. The two are different claims about a recommender, and only the second is homogenization. 3.
